clue.text: I call the regulator: infer I'm badly placed

definitions.note: a clause standing for the phrase: I am a fish out of water

parts.note: to infer is to fish out a conclusion
Ofwat is the body that regulates the water industry in England and Wales
the hesitant noise I make when I call out

explanation.surface: Someone phoning a regulator while feeling out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: Araucaria builds the theme answer from the regulator Ofwat: one who fishes out Ofwat and says er. The wordplay is read back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person uncomfortable in unfamiliar surroundings, which is what being badly placed means.

clue.text: Set off with permit to control outbursts

indicators.note: to control things is to manage and arrange them, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: An official sets things off by issuing a permit meant to keep outbursts in check.
explanation.definitionFit: Fits of temper are sudden angry episodes, exactly the eruptions of rage meant by outbursts.

clue.text: Cut the end off 1 across to take 1 across

indicators.note: taking the end off means a final portion is cut away from the longer word

parts.note: a seabird that takes fish, like every 'I take 1 across' in this puzzle
the end of the long across answer

explanation.surface: An instruction to trim something, cryptically built from the puzzle's theme.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is the shearwater; cutting off WATER, the last word of 1 across, leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To shear is to cut, as with shears clipping wool or hedges.

clue.text: Gold box used by painters and musicians

parts.note: a chest is a large box
the Royal Academy, the body of painters

explanation.surface: A gold box shared by artists and players.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large group of instrumental players, so the collective noun fits musicians.

clue.text: Deal with cars on road

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to trade, often illicitly
second meaning: vehicles moving along streets

explanation.surface: An instruction to handle the cars on the road, like a traffic warden.
explanation.definitionFit: To traffic is to trade in goods, and the noun names the vehicles moving along streets.

clue.text: TV counsellor could be fairer about Zen leader

definitions.note: the TV psychiatrist is usually spelt Frasier

indicators.note: about means around, so the other letters are placed around the single one
something that could be another word is a possible rearrangement of its letters
a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

explanation.surface: A television therapist might seem fairer if he embraced Zen.
explanation.walkthrough: The sitcom character Frasier Crane is a radio psychiatrist; Araucaria spells him with Z to suit the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Frasier is the TV sitcom psychiatrist who gives advice to callers, a counsellor on screen.

clue.text: Everyone's expression is divine

explanation.surface: A claim that what everyone says is heavenly.
explanation.definitionFit: Allah is the Arabic name of God, the supreme deity, so a divine being.

clue.text: Telepathy time? Not when it's twisting the tongue

indicators.note: twisting a word wrenches it out of shape, so its letters are put in a new order

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A question about telepathy, and a tongue twister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' looks like a negative but is just three letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is an invented international language, and tongue is a common word for a language.

clue.text: What may need breaking — no point — I take too many cuppas

indicators.note: no point says a compass direction is to be dropped from the phrase

parts.note: the ice needs breaking at an awkward party
east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone who drinks so much tea they need to break the ice.
explanation.walkthrough: A theic is a rare word for an excessive tea drinker; a cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A theic is someone who drinks too much tea and suffers from it, so a person taking too many cuppas.

clue.text: This 1 across can still see — a clever postscript

parts.note: the indefinite article in its other form

explanation.surface: A fish out of its element that can still see, with a witty afterthought.
explanation.walkthrough: The anableps is the four-eyed fish, whose eyes are split to see above and below the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: This tropical fish has eyes divided to see in air as well as water, so even out of water it keeps its sight.

clue.text: Two years' bedsits may evoke "Don't leave me" from carol singer

indicators.note: to evoke is to call something forth, so the letters are made to produce a new phrase

parts.note: Y twice, Y being the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: Two years of living in bedsits might draw a plea for company from a singer.
explanation.walkthrough: A bedsit is a British one-room rented flat.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a plea for someone to remain close, the same request as asking them not to leave.

clue.text: Breaking of rules of grammar by editor in person?

definitions.note: the grammatical form used by an editor speaking as one

indicators.note: breaking something smashes its order, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An editor who breaks grammatical rules in person.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer itself breaks a rule of grammar, mixing plural our with singular self, which is the editorial we.
explanation.definitionFit: Ourself is the reflexive used with the royal or editorial we, when one person speaks as us.

clue.text: Home bird? I t-take what's coming to me

parts.note: bird is slang for a woman, referred to as her
the stammered letter on its own

explanation.surface: A stammering stay-at-home claiming what is owed.
explanation.definitionFit: To inherit is to receive property due on someone's death, the legacy coming to one.

clue.text: Mog backing it? Not saying

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: Mog is a familiar British name for a pet cat

explanation.surface: A cat supporting something without a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means understood without being stated, so the definition is an adjectival phrase for unspoken.

clue.text: I take 1 across as part of flower or insect

parts.note: the bulb-like underground stem of a plant such as a crocus

explanation.surface: A creature claiming to catch fish as if it were a flower or insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The cormorant is a diving seabird that catches fish, so a creature that takes them.

clue.text: Church line about pollution can't go wrong

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a thing that can't go wrong

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the two-letter line goes around the pollution

explanation.surface: A church rail line surrounded by pollution yet infallible.
explanation.definitionFit: A certainty is a sure thing, something guaranteed that cannot fail or turn out badly.

clue.text: I take 1 across at sea in the Antarctic, under a pound

indicators.note: in a down clue, being under means coming lower in the column, so these pieces follow

parts.note: the abbreviation for a pound in weight
the Ross Sea is off Antarctica

explanation.surface: A seabird fishing in Antarctic waters, weighing under a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece under another sits below it.
explanation.definitionFit: The albatross is a great ocean bird that feeds on fish and squid, so it takes fish.

clue.text: I take 1 across (solution found in a get-together)

indicators.note: found in says one thing sits inside another, so the solution is placed within the meeting

parts.note: a merger is a coming together

explanation.surface: A creature that catches fish, with the answer revealed at a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The merganser is a fish-eating diving duck with a serrated bill, so it takes fish.

clue.text: I take 1 across: beast who does so is about to pull up

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so the animal wraps around the other word

parts.note: a seal is an animal that also catches fish

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: to lug is to pull or drag

explanation.surface: A fish-eater, and another animal that does likewise about to haul something up.
explanation.definitionFit: The gull is a coastal bird that snatches fish from the sea, so it takes fish.

clue.text: Hold back the chorus

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to abstain or restrain oneself
second meaning: the repeated part of a song

explanation.surface: An order to restrain a choir.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means abstain from doing; as a noun it is the repeated lines of a song or poem.

clue.text: I take 1 across (to sound of disapproval by fool)

explanation.surface: A creature that catches fish, jeered at by a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Three ways in: the seabird, the wordplay, and a second definition, since a booby is also a dunce.
explanation.definitionFit: The booby is a tropical seabird that dives for fish, and the word is also old slang for a stupid person.

clue.text: Ear's in, ear out — lovely stuff!

indicators.note: in says the ear adjective is put inside the other piece
out suggests disorder or being put out of place, so the three letters are rearranged

parts.note: otic means relating to the ear

explanation.surface: Something heard in one ear and out the other, described as lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the saying 'in one ear and out the other'.
explanation.definitionFit: Erotica is sexually arousing art or writing, which an admirer might wryly call lovely stuff.

clue.text: How to talk about instincts? Me? Coming up!

parts.note: the id is the instinctive part of the mind in Freud

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means rising from bottom to top, so the French word is read backwards

parts.note: French for me, used jokingly in English

explanation.surface: Someone eager to discuss their own instincts.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a characteristic way of expressing things in a language, a manner of speaking.

clue.text: What Brummel called the Prince, with dire results

definitions.note: read as two words, a fat ally
definitions.meaning: Beau Brummell asked 'Who's your fat friend?' of the Prince Regent
second meaning: in a way that leads to death or disaster

explanation.surface: A dandy's famous insult to a royal that ended badly for him.
explanation.walkthrough: Beau Brummell, a Regency dandy, fell from favour after mocking the Prince Regent as a fat friend; split the answer as FAT ALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatally means in a way causing death or ruin, which matches an outcome with dire consequences.

clue.text: Welsh church organ's first step recorded

definitions.note: sounds like steppe, a grassy plain

parts.note: llan is Welsh for church, as in place names like Llandudno

indicators.note: the possessive first means only the opening letter of the organ is taken

explanation.surface: The first step of a Welsh church organ captured on tape.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a sound pun: step said out loud is steppe, the flat grassland that a llano also is.
explanation.definitionFit: A llano is a vast treeless plain of South America, the counterpart of a steppe.

clue.text: Emperor with a Gallic turn, possibly

indicators.note: possibly means one possible version of the letters, a rearranged form

explanation.surface: A Roman ruler with a French twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Caligula was the third Roman emperor, notorious for his cruelty and extravagance.

clue.text: Beast took a pill — no charge!

indicators.note: no charge means without the fee, so the fee's letters are taken out

parts.note: taken as written; that the beast also runs straight through these words is a coincidence, as no word signals a hidden answer
a toll is a charge for passage

explanation.surface: An animal swallowed a free pill.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of TOLL are scattered through the phrase: T, one O and the final LL go.
explanation.definitionFit: The okapi is an African mammal related to the giraffe, a beast of the Congo forest.

clue.text: Block to let characters from Butlin's get Mondays off

indicators.note: letting characters out of words frees the letters to form something new
off means removed, and the days of the weekday name are what come off

parts.note: Butlin's is a chain of British holiday camps

explanation.surface: Holiday-camp staff are given Mondays free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mondays off' reads as days off, but it is the DAY that comes off, leaving MONS.
explanation.definitionFit: A stumbling stone is an obstacle or hindrance, something that blocks progress.
